questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Mortar joints?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Kostura / Kustura” = mortar joints. Origin: Spanish costura “seam, stitching”. A mortar joint is the seam that stitches the bricks together. The same term is also used for: tool joint.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Brick is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “La Drillo / Ladrilyo” = brick. Origin: Spanish ladrillo “brick”. The source spells it La Drillo, but the real word is ladrillo. The same term is also used for: cement brick.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Putty is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Masilya” = putty. Origin: Spanish masilla “putty”, from masa “dough, paste”.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Rubble?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Eskombro” = rubble. Origin: Spanish escombro “rubble, debris”.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Paint?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Pintura” = paint. Origin: Spanish pintura “paint”, the same root as English “picture” and “paint”.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Masonry fill?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Lastilyas” = masonry fill. Likely borrowed from Spanish lastre “ballast, gravel fill” with a diminutive ending: the gravelly fill. The same term is also used for: earthfill, Mix of cement and gravel.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Varnish finish?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Monyeka” = varnish finish. Likely from Spanish muñeca “doll”, which also names the rag pad used to rub on varnish.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Pea gravel is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Grabita” = pea gravel. Likely origin: Spanish grava “gravel” with a diminutive ending, so “little gravel”.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Earthfill?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Eskumbro / Escombro / Lastilyas” = earthfill. Origin: Spanish escombro “rubble, debris”. The same term is also used for: masonry fill, Mix of cement and gravel.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Plastered course?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Kusturada” = plastered course. Built on kustura (Spanish costura “seam, stitching”): a plastered course is a stitched line of plaster.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Mix of cement and gravel is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Lastilyas” = mix of cement and gravel. Likely borrowed from Spanish lastre “ballast, gravel fill” with a diminutive ending. Memory hook: lastilyas is the gravelly fill mix. The same term is also used for: earthfill, masonry fill.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Cement brick is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Ladrilyo / Landrilyo” = cement brick. Origin: Spanish ladrillo “brick”, with an extra n in the Filipino form. The same term is also used for: brick.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Crushed stone is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Eskondro / Escondro” = crushed stone. Likely a variant of Spanish escombro “rubble”; crushed stone is broken rubble.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Fill?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tambak” = fill. Origin: Tagalog tambak “heap, landfill”.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Plaster of Paris?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Eskayola” = plaster of paris. Origin: Spanish escayola “plaster”, from Italian scagliola. Eskayola is escayola.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Scrapped filler?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Batak” = scrapped filler. Origin not confirmed. Memory hook: the filler is scraped flat, and batak sounds like the “bat-bat” of a scraper.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Filler?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tapal, Dagdag” = filler. Origin: Tagalog tapal “patch, to cover a hole” and dagdag “to add”. A filler is something added to patch.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Scratch coat?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Rebocada” = scratch coat. Likely from Spanish revocar “to plaster, render” (revoque = plaster coat). The exact form is unconfirmed.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Tool joint is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Kostura / Kustura” = tool joint. Origin: Spanish costura “seam, stitching”. A mortar joint is the seam that stitches the bricks together. The same term is also used for: mortar joints.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to CHB laying?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Asinta” = CHB laying. Origin: likely Spanish asentar “to set in place”. Laying blocks means setting them on the wall.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Pick work?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Piketa” = pick work. Origin: Spanish piqueta “pick, mason's hammer”. Same root as English “pick”.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Mortar is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Paupo” = mortar. Origin not confirmed. Memory hook: paupo sounds like pa-upo “for sitting”: bricks sit on the mortar.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Concrete slab (rough slab)?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Larga Masa” = concrete slab (rough slab). Origin: Spanish larga “long, large” + masa “mass, mix, dough”: a large mass of concrete mix.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Plaster (stucco)?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Palitada” = plaster (stucco). Origin: Spanish paletada “a trowelful”, from paleta “trowel”. Plaster is applied with a trowel.
